subject: Cloud Computing
title: The GitLab Database Deletion
description: A quick, practical guide to The GitLab Database Deletion.

hook.text: On January 31, 2017, a GitLab engineer accidentally deleted the production database. Six hours of data vanished.

buildup.text: The engineer was troubleshooting database replication late at night. Fatigue led to a command on the wrong server.

discovery.text: GitLab tried five different backup methods. None worked properly. The only usable backup was six hours old.

twist.text: GitLab live-streamed the recovery on YouTube. Radical transparency turned a disaster into a trust-building moment.

climax.text: After recovery, GitLab overhauled its backup strategy. The incident became a teaching moment for the industry.

punchline.text: Five backup methods. None worked. Test your backups.

quiz.question: What was unique about GitLab's response to their data loss?
options: They live-streamed the recovery effort publicly on YouTube
They blamed the cloud provider and demanded compensation
They shut down the company permanently after the incident

details.summary: In 2017, a GitLab engineer accidentally deleted a production database during maintenance. Five backup methods all failed or were misconfigured, and only a lucky six-hour-old snapshot saved the company from total data loss. GitLab live-streamed the recovery.
details.whyItMatters: GitLab's incident proved that untested backups are not backups at all. It became a landmark case study for why backup verification and disaster recovery testing are non-negotiable.
takeaways: Five backup methods all failed when needed
Only a lucky recent snapshot prevented total data loss
GitLab live-streamed recovery, setting a transparency standard

faq.question: Why did all GitLab backups fail?
faq.answer: PostgreSQL backups were silently failing due to version mismatches, LVM snapshots were not configured, the staging database was stale, and replication to secondary databases was paused. None of the backup methods had been recently tested for actual restorability.

faq.question: What lesson is most important from the GitLab incident?
faq.answer: Test your backups regularly by actually restoring them. Backups that have never been restored are assumptions, not safeguards. GitLab now conducts regular restore drills and published detailed incident reports that became essential reading for the industry.
